attachment.content:
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.
SKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a pull request
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

All experiments use English-language datasets; cross-lingual generalization remains untested.

Our supervised approaches (DeBERTa verifier, hidden state probes, MLP/RF on signal combinations) all fail to close the oracle gap; whether content-aware verifiers with access to task-specific structure could succeed remains open.

We evaluate at $N{=}8$ (primary) and $N{=}16$; behavior at larger sample sizes is unknown (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}).
The free-form ablation covers SciERC NER and CoNLL NER with one model; RE free-form results are in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}.
Qwen3-8B's SciERC checkpoint used empty \texttt{<think></think>} blocks; a three-part analysis rules out this confound (Appendix~\ref{app:thinking_token}).
LP compression worsens on easy datasets at lower temperature (CoNLL tied fractions reach 95.8\% at $T{=}0.7$); whether reduced temperature translates to selection gains remains untested.
We tested verbalized confidence \cite{lin2022teaching, tian2023calibration} as a second per-sample signal; it exhibits severe overconfidence (mean 8.58/10 on SciERC, 9.24/10 on CoNLL) and yields the weakest QE and selection among all signals (Appendix~\ref{app:verbalized_confidence}).
Ad-hoc LP${\times}$VC combinations yield at most $+0.2$~pp over greedy (not significant; \S\ref{sec:discussion}); whether \textit{learned} combinations could close the gap remains open.
The $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ threshold used for tied/non-tied LP stratification is a post-hoc exploratory choice; while selection F1 is stable across $\varepsilon \in [0, 0.2]$ (Appendix~\ref{app:epsilon_robustness}), the specific subset gains should be interpreted as characterizing the compression phenomenon rather than as a tuned selection strategy.
We tested one remedy for LP compression (entity-token-only LP, excluding format/schema tokens) which fails to improve selection despite increasing within-instance variance on SciERC ($4{\times}$); LP${\times}$VC combinations also fail to recover selection (\S\ref{sec:discussion}). Our supervised signal combination baseline uses only the five unsupervised signals studied; a DeBERTa verifier encoding input-output pairs also fails to close the gap (preliminary, SciERC $n{=}106$), hidden state probes on the generating model's representations improve correlation ($+37$\% on SciERC) but do not improve selection (gap closure $-5.1$\%; Appendix~\ref{app:hidden_probe}), ; the bottleneck extends to model-internal access. Entity embeddings and calibration-based approaches remain untested.
Other per-sample scoring methods exist but were not evaluated: Self-Certainty \cite{kang2025selfcertainty} (consistency of token-level self-evaluation) and P(True) \cite{kadavath2022language} (model's own probability estimate of correctness) both produce per-sample scores and could in principle address the alignment bottleneck; whether they suffer from similar compression under fine-tuning is unknown.

97	On SciERC ($n{=}529$, 2-seed sign tests\footnote{MDE${\approx}$1.5~pp at 80\% power ($n{=}529$); Few-NERD ($n{=}32{,}565$; MDE${\approx}$0.22~pp) provides the definitive test.}), the oracle (0.775) reveals 13.0~pp of headroom, but LP achieves $+0.2$~pp ($p{=}0.29$), below the MDE (${\approx}$1.5~pp); selection effects below this threshold cannot be reliably detected.
98	The pattern holds across CoNLL and WNUT-17 (Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection}); under stringent TOST anchors, some configurations show significant \textit{degradation} (Appendix~\ref{app:tost}).
99	Few-NERD provides the definitive contrast: LP achieves $+1.39$~pp ($p{<}0.001$) at low degeneracy (\S\ref{sec:fewnerd}), while structural signals still degrade selection.
100	
101	\paragraph{Qualitative factors governing selection effectiveness.}
102	Three factors qualitatively shape LP selection gains: (1)~\textit{instance degeneracy} compresses the candidate space, leaving fewer instances where any signal can improve over greedy (SciERC 17.8\%, CoNLL 48.4\%; Table~\ref{tab:fewnerd}); (2)~\textit{oracle headroom} bounds the maximum achievable gain (CoNLL ${\approx}2$\,pp vs.\ SciERC 13.1\,pp); (3)~\textit{LP-quality alignment}, measured as within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$, determines whether LP can discriminate candidates in the remaining non-degenerate instances (Few-NERD $\rho{\approx}0.5$--$0.7$ vs.\ SciERC $\rho{\approx}0.26$).
103	These factors are consistent with the observed pattern (Table~\ref{tab:fewnerd}): Few-NERD (low degeneracy, strong alignment) shows the largest LP gain ($+1.39$\,pp), SciERC (weak alignment) shows unreliable gains ($+0.04{\pm}0.48$\,pp, 3-seed; Table~\ref{tab:multiseed}), CoNLL (high degeneracy, minimal headroom) shows no gain, and WNUT-17 represents the signal-collapse boundary: LP $\rho{=}{-}0.446$ (the model assigns higher log-probabilities to confidently wrong outputs), within-instance alignment absent ($\rho{=}0.043$, n.s.), and construction ineffective ($p{>}0.05$, mixed sign) because 51\% of instances yield F1${=}0$.
104	Yet QE remains effective on WNUT-17 (VC $\rho{=}0.730$; Table~\ref{tab:wnut}), confirming QE-selection decoupling at this boundary.
105	This characterization is qualitative: the three factors do not combine into a predictive model ($R^2{<}0$ across 23 configurations), but each factor's role is individually supported by controlled ablations (\S\ref{sec:fewnerd}, \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
